ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::0: For several decades, regulatory testing schemes for genetic damage have been standardized where the tests being utilized examined mutations and structural and numerical chromosomal damage. ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::1: Nutritional supplements may improve development of infants born small (preterm or small for gestational age [SGA]) but may increase the risk of later metabolic disease. ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::2: Objectives Recently, two point-of-care (PoC) feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV) antibody test kits (Witness and Anigen Rapid) were reported as being able to differentiate FIV-vaccinated from FIV-infected cats at a single time point, irrespective of the gap between testing and last vaccination (0-7 years). ideas_up_v2.xsum::47: David Poole told Cardiff Crown Court he trapped Adnan Khalid, 27, who was charged with grooming a 14-year-old. ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::3: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is a rare monogenic disorder characterized by benign tumors in multiple organs as well as a high prevalence of epilepsy, intellectual disability and autism. ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::4: Silica nanoparticles (nanoSiO 2 ) are promising systems that can deliver biologically active compounds to tissues such as the heart in a controllable manner. This article explores the ex vivo heart function and mitochondria after exposure to nanoSiO 2 to elucidate these mechanisms. The cumulative administration of nanoSiO 2 reduced the mechanical performance index of the rat heart with a half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC 50 ) of 93 μg/mL. The relaxation rate was specifically affected by nanoparticle exposure. In isolated mitochondria nanoSiO 2 was found to be internalized through direct observation. Oxidative phosphorylation was inhibited by the internalized nanoparticles. The mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨ m ) was significantly reduced following nanoSiO 2 treatment. The mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) was induced with an increasing dose of nanoSiO 2 . Cyclosporine A (CsA), a potent blocker of the mPTP, partially recovered the pore dysfunction. ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::5: Return to play (RTP) of National Football League (NFL) athletes after isolated anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears has been reported. ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::6: Pulmonary hypertension in response to exercise is a marker of the hemodynamic severity of mitral stenosis (MS). ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::8: The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2) has led to a significant number of mortalities worldwide. ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::7: The relationship between chronic liver disease and COVID-19 patient outcomes remains poorly understood. Our investigation focused on determining whether liver conditions influence mortality rates in hospitalized COVID-19 cases. ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::9: Temperature and water availability are two of the most important variables affecting all aspects of an anuran's key physiological processes such as body temperature (T b), evaporative water loss (EWL) and standard metabolic rate (SMR). Consequently, researchers should interpret the role of M b within the framework of both physiological mechanisms and habitat-specific selective pressures. ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::12: Open fractures are contaminated wounds that contain gram-positive and gram-negative organisms; therefore, wide-spectrum antibiotic therapy should be incorporated into the treatment plan. An antibiotic bead pouch and vacuum-assisted wound closure may help reduce the risk for secondary and nosocomial contamination and subsequent infection. The formulation of a soft-tissue treatment plan must occur during the initial wound assessment and the initial fixation of an open fracture and should not be considered a secondary or consecutive process. ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::10: Chronotaraxis is an impairment of the perception of the sequencing of time. Functional connectivity between the thalamus and prefrontal cortex appears particularly vulnerable to ischaemic injury. Rehabilitation strategies targeting temporal orientation may improve outcomes in affected patients. Cognitive training programs have shown promise in restoring some aspects of temporal perception. The prognosis varies depending on the extent of thalamic involvement and the timeliness of intervention. Early thrombolytic therapy may limit infarct size and preserve function. Multidisciplinary care teams provide optimal management for these complex neurological presentations.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::11: Some infectious diseases, such as influenza, tuberculosis, and SARS-CoV-2, may be transmitted when virus-laden particles expelled from an infectious person are inhaled by someone else, which is known as the airborne transmission route. These virus-laden particles are more concentrated in the expiratory jet of an infectious person than elsewhere in a well-mixed room. This near-field enhancement in virion exposure has not been well quantified in previous research. Transmission of airborne viruses depends on factors that are inherently variable and, in many cases, poorly constrained. Quantifying this uncertainty requires large ensembles of model simulations that span the variability in input parameters. Models that are well-suited to simulate the near-field evolution of respiratory particles are also computationally expensive. This computational cost limits the exploration of parametric uncertainty in transmission modeling. We developed the Quadrature-based model of Respiratory Aerosol and Droplets (QuaRAD) to perform many simulations spanning the wide variability in factors governing airborne transmission. QuaRAD is an efficient framework for simulating the evolution of virus-laden particles after they are expelled from an infectious person. The model also simulates deposition of particles to the nasal cavity of a susceptible person. QuaRAD calculates the subsequent risk of initial infection following particle deposition. We simulated 10,000 scenarios to quantify the risk of initial infection by SARS-CoV-2 specifically. The predicted risk of infection was highly variable among scenarios. In each scenario, infection risk was strongly enhanced near the infectious individual compared to far-field exposure. In more than 50% of scenarios, the physical distancing needed to avoid near-field enhancements in airborne transmission exceeded two meters. The recommended safe distance of two meters (six feet) was insufficient when the infectious person is not wearing a mask. The distance defining the near-field extent was highly variable among scenarios, ranging considerably across different conditions. The variability in the near-field extent is explained predominantly by variability in expiration velocity among individuals. Expiration velocity determines how far respiratory particles travel before dispersing into the room environment. Our findings suggest that maintaining at least two meters of distance from an infectious person greatly reduces exposure to airborne virions. Protections against airborne transmission, such as N95 respirators, should be available when distancing is not possible in practical settings.

PURPOSE: Cyclical patterns of compliance have been observed with many health-related activities such as dieting and exercise. Whether such patterns exist among users of chronic medications remains unexplored. This study estimates the percentage of patients who restart osteoporosis therapy after a prolonged lapse in medication use. We also identify factors associated with a return to compliance after treatment interruption.

METHODS: We studied 26,636 new users of osteoporosis medications including alendronate, calcitonin, estrogen, raloxifene, or risedronate. All participants were age 65 or older at study entry. An extended lapse in refill compliance was defined as a period of at least 60 days after completing one prescription without obtaining any refill for osteoporosis medication. Survival curves estimated the length of time until therapy resumption occurred. Cox proportional hazards analysis assessed associations between patient characteristics and the rate of resuming treatment. A case crossover analysis examined whether certain events occurring during follow-up triggered a return to refill compliance.

RESULTS: Among patients who stopped therapy for at least 60 days, an estimated 30% restarted treatment within 6 months. Approximately 50% of these patients restarted within 2 years of their treatment gap. A subgroup of patients had at least 6 months of continuous use before their interruption in treatment (n=5863). In this subgroup, 42% restarted therapy within 6 months. Within 2 years, 59% of this subgroup had resumed medication use. Younger patients showed higher rates of returning after a break in medication use. Women were more likely to return compared to men. Those with a history of fracture demonstrated increased likelihood of treatment resumption. Recent hip fractures predicted a return to treatment during the follow-up period. Discharges from nursing homes also predicted treatment resumption. Bone mineral density testing was associated with patients restarting their medications.

CONCLUSION: Extended gaps in treatment are common among users of osteoporosis medications. The effectiveness of these drugs when used in an interrupted manner remains unknown. Compliance interventions should emphasize the need for continuous medication use. Further research must understand why patients often go for months without refilling prescriptions. Whether similar utilization patterns exist for other chronic medications requires additional investigation.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::15: We investigate the reason for the quantum speedup -- quantum algorithms requiring fewer computation steps than their classical counterparts. We extend their representation to the process of setting the problem. The initial measurement selects a setting at random, Bob (the problem setter) unitarily changes it into the desired one. This representation is accessible to Bob and any external observer. Alice (the problem solver) cannot access this representation because it would reveal the function computed by the black box. The function must remain hidden inside the black box from Alice's perspective. We resort to relational quantum mechanics as our theoretical framework. To Alice, the projection of the quantum state due to the initial measurement is retarded at the end of her problem solving action. The algorithm input state remains one of complete ignorance of the setting from her viewpoint. Through black box computations, she unitarily sends this state into the output state. The output state encodes the corresponding solution for each possible setting. The final measurement acquires these solutions. We demonstrate that the final measurement can select any part -- say the R-th part -- of the random outcome of the initial measurement. This selection projects the input state to Alice on a state of lower entropy. In this lower entropy state, she knows a corresponding part of the problem setting. The quantum algorithm is a sum over classical histories. In each history, Alice knows in advance one of the R-th parts of the setting. She performs the black box computations still required to identify the solution in each history. This retrocausality model provides the number of black box computations required to solve an oracle problem for a given value of R. Conversely, the model yields the value of R that explains the speedup of a known quantum algorithm. Setting R = 1/2 always yields the number of black box computations required by an existing quantum algorithm. The same value provides the order of magnitude of the number required by an optimal algorithm.

1917 - Britain conquers Palestine from the Ottoman Empire during World War I. The British government issues the Balfour Declaration, expressing support for establishing "a national home for the Jewish people" in Palestine. The declaration includes a provision that "nothing shall be done which may prejudice the civil and religious rights of existing non-Jewish communities" in the territory. 

1918 - The first significant Palestinian Arab nationalist organizations begin to emerge in response to political changes. The Muntada al-Adabi focuses mainly on cultural activities and Arab identity. The Nadi al-Arabi operates from Damascus and promotes pan-Arab political goals.

1920 - The San Remo conference of Allied Powers formally grants Palestine to Britain as a mandate territory. Britain receives the mandate with the explicit purpose of preparing Palestine for eventual self-rule. Jerusalem experiences violent riots as Palestinian Arabs protest against the implementation of the Balfour Declaration. These riots mark an important assertion of a distinct Palestinian Arab national identity separate from broader Arab or Ottoman identities.

1921 - The British authorities appoint Mohammed Amin al-Husseini as Grand Mufti of Jerusalem. Al-Husseini comes from one of the leading Palestinian Arab families with significant social influence. As leader of the Muslim community, he uses his position to rally Arabs and Muslims throughout the region. His primary political goal becomes preventing any further concessions to Jewish immigration or land purchases.

1922 - A Palestinian Arab delegation formally rejects a British proposal to establish a Legislative Council for Palestine. The delegation states that including the terms of the Balfour Declaration in the draft constitution makes the proposal unacceptable. This rejection demonstrates Palestinian Arab unwillingness to participate in governance structures that legitimize Zionist goals.

1929 - Arab rioters attack Jewish communities, killing approximately 200 Jews in Jerusalem's Old City and the ancient Jewish community of Hebron. British military forces intervene to suppress the widespread riots across Palestine. During their suppression operations, British troops kill 116 Arabs in Jerusalem alone. The violence reflects escalating tensions over Jewish immigration and land purchases.

1930 - The British government issues a White Paper addressing the deteriorating situation in Palestine. A Royal Commission investigates the causes of the 1929 riots and their aftermath. Both the White Paper and the Commission recommend imposing strict limits on Jewish immigration to reduce Arab-Jewish tensions.

1930-35 - Sheikh Izz al-Din al-Qassam establishes and leads the Black Hand, an Islamist militant group. The organization launches a sustained campaign of violence targeting both the Jewish community and British colonial rule. Al-Qassam's activities inspire later Palestinian armed resistance movements and he becomes a martyr figure after his death in 1935.

1935 - The Palestinian Arab leadership reverses its earlier position and accepts the British High Commissioner's revised proposal for a Legislative Assembly. However, the British House of Commons in London rejects the proposal the following year. This rejection eliminates a potential path toward Palestinian Arab participation in governance structures.

1936-39 - The Arab revolt begins with a general strike initiated in the port city of Jaffa. Britain responds by declaring martial law throughout Palestine to restore order. The British authorities dissolve the Arab Higher Committee led by Grand Mufti Al-Husseini. More than 5,000 Arabs are killed during the British military suppression of the revolt. An additional 15,000 Arabs suffer injuries during the three years of conflict. Al-Husseini flees to French-controlled Syria to escape arrest by British authorities.

1947 - The United Nations proposes a partition plan dividing Palestine into separate Jewish and Arab states. The plan designates Jerusalem and its surrounding areas for international control under UN administration. Britain signals its intention to end the Palestine Mandate, making partition the proposed solution. The Arab High Committee categorically rejects the partition plan, refusing to accept a Jewish state on any part of Palestine.

1948 - Israel declares its independence as the British mandate officially ends on May 14. Arab armies from Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Lebanon, and Iraq invade the newly declared state. The Arab forces fail to defeat the Israeli military despite initial expectations of victory. Jordan occupies and later annexes the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the fighting. Egypt establishes military administration over the Gaza Strip. Israel controls the remainder of Mandate Palestine, including West Jerusalem and significant additional territory beyond the UN partition borders. At least 750,000 Palestinian Arabs either flee the fighting or are forcibly expelled from their homes. Disputes over whether the Palestinians left voluntarily or were expelled continue to generate intense controversy. The United Nations establishes the Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA). UNRWA assumes responsibility for providing educational and health services to Palestinian refugees. The agency's mandate extends to Palestinian refugees and their descendants throughout the Middle East. More than four million Palestinians currently live with refugee status in various Arab countries. Many Palestinian refugees remain marginalized in host countries and confined to refugee camps. Slideshow features document conditions inside Shatila refugee camp in Lebanon.

1949-1950s - Fedayeen Palestinian guerrilla fighters establish bases in Egyptian-controlled Gaza and begin raids into Israel. The Egyptian government actively encourages these cross-border attacks against Israeli targets. Fedayeen activity increases significantly after pan-Arab nationalist officers seize power in Cairo through the 1952 revolution.

1956-1957 - Israel secretly colludes with Britain and France to invade Egypt during the Suez Crisis. One of Israel's goals is ending the Fedayeen incursions from Gaza. A UN buffer force deploys to the Sinai Peninsula and Gaza following international pressure. The presence of UN peacekeepers drastically reduces the number of raids into Israel.

1959 - Yasser Arafat founds Fatah, a new Palestinian fighting organization, while living in Egypt. Fatah's primary purpose is conducting armed raids into Israeli territory from neighboring Arab countries.

1964 - The Arab League creates the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) as an umbrella political body. The League simultaneously establishes the Palestine Liberation Army as a military force. Ahmad Shukeiri becomes the first chairman of the PLO.

1967 June - The Six-Day War results in Israel occupying East Jerusalem, the entire West Bank, Gaza Strip, Syria's Golan Heights, and Egypt's Sinai Peninsula. Jewish settlement construction begins in all of these newly occupied territories in the following years. The Israeli government officially approves and supports the settlement enterprise.

1969 - Yasser Arafat assumes leadership of the PLO following his military prominence. His reputation grew from clashes with Israeli forces in Jordan during 1968. Arafat successfully asserts the PLO's independence from Egyptian government control.

1970 - Growing tension develops over the PLO's increasing military and political strength within Jordan. The situation escalates into the Black September clashes between PLO forces and the Jordanian army. King Hussein's forces drive the PLO out of Jordan, forcing the organization into exile. The PLO relocates its headquarters and military forces to southern Lebanon.

1970s-1980s - The PLO and other armed Palestinian groups adopt international terrorism tactics. Airline hijackings become a favored method for gaining international attention. Palestinian groups attack Israeli soldiers, officials, and civilians both within Israel and in foreign countries. These operations aim to highlight the Palestinian cause to the world. Leila Khaled participates in multiple hijackings that focus international media attention on Palestinian demands. Profile features examine the motivations and backgrounds of hijackers. On This Day historical feature recalls 1970 when guerrillas destroyed multiple commercial jets.

1972 - The Palestinian "Black September" organization takes Israeli Olympic athletes hostage in Munich. Gunmen murder two athletes at the Olympic Village during the initial attack. Nine more Israeli athletes die during a failed rescue attempt by German authorities at the airport. Israel launches a covert operation of reprisal assassinations targeting those responsible for planning the Munich attack.

1973 - Israeli forces raid PLO bases in Beirut and southern Lebanon before the October war begins. Additional raids continue during the Yom Kippur War, known to Arabs as the Ramadan War.

1974 April-May - Two hardline Palestinian factions carry out attacks inside northern Israel. The Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine General Command conducts one operation. The Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine executes another raid. Militants kill 43 Israeli civilians, including numerous children, during an attack on an apartment block in Kiryat Shmona. Another attack targets a school in Maalot, resulting in additional civilian deaths.

1974 June - Following the 1973 war, the PLO adopts its Ten-Point Programme representing a significant policy shift. The programme allows for compromise with Israel as a step toward establishing complete Palestinian control over historic Palestine. The ultimate goal remains gaining control over all territory including present-day Israel. Several hardline factions reject this gradualist approach and split away. These groups form the Rejectionist Front opposed to any compromise with Israel. The Rejectionist Front intensifies attacks on Israeli military personnel and civilians.

1974 October - The Arab League formally recognizes the PLO as the "sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people." The League grants the PLO full membership status. Yasser Arafat serves for many years as the controversial icon of Palestinians' struggle with Israel. BBC Obituary provides comprehensive coverage of Yasser Arafat's life and legacy. The Economist publishes analysis of Arafat's historical impact.

1974 November - Yasser Arafat becomes the first non-state leader invited to address the United Nations General Assembly. He delivers his famous speech declaring he carries "an olive branch and a freedom fighter's gun." The speech challenges the UN to choose between supporting Palestinian rights or maintaining the status quo.

1975 - The Rejectionist Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine collaborates with a German far-left armed group. Together they hijack an Air France plane flying from Israel to France. The hijackers divert the aircraft to Entebbe airport in Uganda. Israeli commandos execute a daring long-distance rescue operation. The Israeli forces successfully rescue most passengers and crew members. All hijackers are killed during the Entebbe raid.

1977 May - The right-wing Likud party achieves a surprise election victory in Israel, ending decades of Labor Party dominance. The new Likud government actively encourages and expands Jewish settlement construction on the West Bank and in Gaza.

1978 March - PLO militants conduct an attack along Israel's coastal road that kills 38 Israeli civilians. Israel responds with its first major military incursion into southern Lebanon. Israeli forces drive the PLO and other Palestinian armed groups out of the border region.

1978 September - Israel pledges to expand Palestinian self-government in the West Bank and Gaza. This commitment forms part of the Camp David Accords negotiated with Egypt. The Accords establish full diplomatic relations between Israel and Egypt, the first Arab country to recognize Israel.

1982 June - Israel launches a full-scale invasion of Lebanon with the goal of expelling PLO leadership from Beirut. The invasion follows an assassination attempt on Israel's ambassador to London by a Palestinian faction. PLO leaders are forced to evacuate Lebanon under international supervision. Israel's occupation of Lebanon sees the relocation of PLO headquarters to Tunisia. Video documentation captures the Sabra and Shatila massacre. BBC Witness programme provides testimony about the 1982 events.

1982 September - Christian Phalangist militias allied with Israel massacre Palestinians in Beirut's Sabra and Shatila refugee camps. Estimates of the death toll range from hundreds to thousands. The PLO leadership relocates its headquarters to Tunis, Tunisia. The organization remains in Tunisia until moving to Gaza in 1994.

1985 October - The Israeli air force conducts a long-range strike on PLO headquarters in Tunis. The raid comes after a PLO group kills three Israeli tourists on a yacht in Cyprus. The Palestine Liberation Front, a PLO faction, hijacks the Italian cruise ship Achille Lauro. Hijackers demand the release of 50 Palestinians held in Israeli prisons. The hijackers murder Leon Klinghoffer, an elderly American passenger in a wheelchair, pushing him overboard.

1987 December - The First Palestinian Intifada uprising erupts spontaneously in the Palestinian Territories. The Muslim Brotherhood's Gaza branch forms Hamas, the Islamic Resistance Movement. Hamas rapidly transitions from social services to armed violence against Israel.

1988 - Jordan formally abandons its claim to sovereignty over the West Bank. King Hussein cedes Jordan's claim to the PLO as the representative of Palestinians. The Palestinian National Council convenes in Algiers and proclaims the existence of a State of Palestine. The declaration asserts Palestinian statehood despite lacking control over territory.

1990 - The PLO leadership backs Iraq following its invasion and annexation of Kuwait. Kuwait severs diplomatic and financial ties with the PLO in response. Kuwait subsequently expels approximately 400,000 Palestinian residents as collective punishment.

1991 October - A US-Soviet sponsored international conference convenes in Madrid, Spain. The conference brings Israeli and Palestinian representatives together for face-to-face negotiations. These talks represent the first direct Israeli-Palestinian negotiations since 1949.

1992 - The Israeli Labour government led by Yitzhak Rabin takes office. Rabin pledges to halt the expansion of Jewish settlements in occupied territories. The government begins secret back-channel negotiations with PLO representatives in Oslo, Norway.

1993 September - Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and PLO Chairman Yasser Arafat sign the Oslo Declaration of Principles. The agreement establishes a framework for Palestinian self-government in stages. The Oslo Accords formally end the First Intifada, which had been losing momentum since the Madrid Conference. Violence continues from various Palestinian groups that reject the Oslo process and oppose compromise with Israel.

1994 February - Baruch Goldstein, a member of the extremist Jewish Kach movement, massacres 29 Palestinians. The victims are killed while praying at the Cave of the Patriarchs shrine in Hebron on the West Bank. The massacre temporarily derails the peace process and sparks Palestinian protests.

1994 May-July - Israel withdraws its military forces from most of Gaza and from the West Bank city of Jericho. Yasser Arafat relocates from Tunis to Gaza and establishes the Palestinian National Authority. The Palestinian National Authority assumes limited self-government responsibilities in areas of Israeli withdrawal.

1994 December - Yasser Arafat shares the Nobel Peace Prize with Israeli leaders Yitzhak Rabin and Foreign Minister Shimon Peres. The award recognizes their efforts toward achieving peace in the Middle East.

1995 - The Interim Agreement between Israel and the PLO establishes a detailed path for transferring additional power and territory. The agreement forms the basis for subsequent negotiations including the 1997 Hebron Protocol. The Wye River Memorandum of 1998 builds on the Interim Agreement framework. The internationally-sponsored "Road Map for Peace" of 2003 also derives from these earlier agreements.

2000-2001 - Negotiations between Israeli Labour Prime Minister Ehud Barak and Yasser Arafat collapse at Camp David. Disputes center on the timing and extent of proposed further Israeli withdrawals from the West Bank. Palestinian protests against the stalled negotiations escalate into a new armed Intifada, later called the Second Intifada or Al-Aqsa Intifada.

2001 December - Israel deploys troops to encircle the West Bank city of Ramallah following a series of deadly Palestinian attacks. Yasser Arafat becomes confined to his government compound in Ramallah, unable to leave the besieged area.

2002 March - The Israeli army launches Operation Defensive Shield, a major military offensive across the West Bank. Israel begins construction of a separation barrier in the West Bank, stating its purpose is preventing armed Palestinians from entering Israel. The route of the barrier generates controversy as it frequently deviates from the pre-1967 ceasefire line. Large sections of the barrier extend into West Bank territory, effectively annexing land.

2002 March - An Arab League summit meeting in Beirut proposes a comprehensive peace initiative. The Arab League offers to recognize Israel in exchange for complete withdrawal from all territories occupied since 1967. The proposal calls for agreement on establishing a Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its capital. The initiative demands a "fair solution" to the Palestinian refugee question based on UN resolutions. This becomes known as the Arab League Peace Plan or Arab Peace Initiative.

2003 March - Yasser Arafat creates the new post of prime minister within the Palestinian Authority structure. He appoints Fatah veteran Mahmoud Abbas to the position to lead contacts with the United States and Israel. Both the US and Israel refuse to conduct negotiations with Arafat himself, citing his alleged support for terrorism.

2003 May - Israeli Prime Minister Ariel Sharon makes a significant statement acknowledging that Israeli occupation of Palestinian territories cannot continue indefinitely. This represents a notable shift in rhetoric from the leader of the Likud party.

2003 June - An Arab League meeting in Egypt expresses support for the internationally-proposed "road map" peace plan. The road map is jointly proposed by the United States, European Union, Russia, and United Nations (the "Quartet"). The Palestinian National Authority officially accepts the road map framework. Israel also accepts the road map, though with significant reservations. The plan envisions an independent Palestinian state and requires freezing Jewish settlement construction on the West Bank.

2003 September - Mahmoud Abbas resigns as Palestinian prime minister after only four months in office. He cites US and Israeli intransigence as major obstacles to progress. Abbas also faces significant internal Palestinian opposition to his government and policies. Fatah veteran Ahmed Qurei succeeds Abbas as prime minister.

2004 March - Israeli forces assassinate Sheikh Ahmed Yassin, the founder and spiritual leader of Hamas. Yassin is killed by a missile strike while leaving a mosque in Gaza.

2004 April - Israel assassinates Abd al-Aziz al-Rantissi, who had succeeded Yassin as Hamas leader. Rantissi is killed only weeks after assuming leadership of the organization.

2004 July - The International Court of Justice issues an advisory opinion on the Israeli separation barrier. The Court rules that the barrier violates international law in its current route. The opinion states that the barrier must be removed and Palestinians compensated for damages.

2004 November - Yasser Arafat dies in a hospital in Paris, France. He had traveled to France in October for urgent medical treatment for an undiagnosed illness. Speculation and conspiracy theories about the cause of his death persist for years.

2005 January - Mahmoud Abbas wins election as Yasser Arafat's successor to head the Palestinian National Authority. Abbas campaigns on a platform of negotiation rather than armed resistance.

2005 September - Israel implements its unilateral disengagement plan from the Gaza Strip. All Jewish settlements in Gaza are evacuated and demolished. Israel withdraws all military personnel from inside Gaza. However, Israel retains control over Gaza's airspace, seaports, and most border crossings. This continued control leads to debates over whether the occupation truly ended.

2006 March - The Hamas Islamist movement's candidate Ismail Haniyeh forms a government after Hamas wins parliamentary elections in January. A power struggle for primacy with Fatah begins immediately. The United States and European Union suspend financial aid to the Palestinian Authority government. Israel ends the transfer of tax revenues it collects on behalf of Palestinians. The international community takes these actions because Hamas refuses to recognize Israel, renounce violence, or accept previous peace accords. The Islamist movement's victory in legislative council elections surprises international observers. Hamas has controlled Gaza since 2006 and proved itself a formidable adversary. The organization fights both against Israel and rival Palestinian factions. Explainer articles detail who Hamas is and its ideology.

2006 June - Hamas militants operating from Gaza capture Israeli soldier Gilad Shalit near a border crossing. Shalit is held hostage for five years while Hamas demands release of Palestinian prisoners. Major military clashes erupt between Israeli forces and Hamas fighters in Gaza. Israel imposes strict restrictions on the movement of goods and people into and out of Gaza.

2006 September - Armed clashes break out between Fatah and Hamas supporters in Gaza. Various Arab states attempt to mediate between the rival Palestinian factions. Palestinian groups themselves seek to broker ceasefires to avert full-scale civil war. Mediation efforts continue for months with limited success.

2007 March - Fatah and Hamas agree to form a national unity government following negotiations in Mecca. The agreement aims to end months of intermittent violent clashes in Gaza between the factions.

2007 June - The national unity government collapses after only three months. Hamas stages a military takeover and violently ousts Fatah forces from Gaza. Hamas reinforces its exclusive control over the Gaza Strip. Israel responds by tightening its blockade following an increase in rocket attacks from Gaza. Egypt closes its border crossing with Gaza at Rafah. Mahmoud Abbas appoints Salam Fayyad as prime minister of a West Bank-based government. Hamas refuses to recognize Fayyad's authority or government. Two rival Palestinian governments emerge, one governing the West Bank and another controlling Gaza. The United States and European Union resume financial aid exclusively to Fayyad's West Bank government.

2007 November - A US-hosted international conference convenes in Annapolis, Maryland. For the first time, the "two-state solution" is formally established as the basis for future Israeli-Palestinian negotiations. The conference brings together Israeli and Palestinian leaders with international participation.

2008 March - Efforts at reconciliation between Fatah and Hamas begin with talks in Yemen. The next round of reconciliation talks takes place in Cairo in November. The Cairo talks stall when Hamas objects to Fatah's continued arrest of Hamas activists on the West Bank. Mutual recriminations prevent progress toward Palestinian unity.

2008 November - Israel launches a military incursion into Gaza to destroy smuggling tunnels. Hamas views the operation as a violation of an informal ceasefire. Hamas responds by launching rockets toward Israeli civilian areas.

2008 December - Israel initiates Operation Cast Lead, a major month-long invasion of Gaza. The stated goal is stopping Hamas and other militant groups from firing rockets into Israel. Israeli forces conduct extensive air strikes followed by a ground invasion.

2010 February - Fatah and Hamas resume talks on national reconciliation after years of division. Direct negotiations also resume between Israel and the Palestinian Authority. However, talks falter over the contentious question of continued Jewish settlement construction.

2010 May - Israeli naval forces intercept a flotilla of ships attempting to break the maritime blockade of Gaza. Nine Turkish pro-Palestinian activists are killed during Israel's capture of the vessels. The incident causes international outrage and severely strains Israeli-Turkish relations. Q&A features explain the raid on the Mavi Marmara ship.

2011 April-May - Fatah and Hamas reach agreement at talks in Cairo to form a unity government. The parties pledge to hold fresh Palestinian elections within a year. However, no practical implementation of the unity agreement follows due to continued mutual distrust.

2011 - The Palestinian National Authority launches a diplomatic campaign for UN membership of a "State of Palestine." The campaign aims to highlight stalled peace talks with Israel and gain international recognition. The bid for full UN membership fails due to lack of Security Council support. UNESCO, the UN cultural agency, accepts Palestine as a member in October despite US opposition.

2012 May - Following preliminary discussions in Qatar, Fatah and Hamas sign the Cairo Agreement. The agreement pledges both factions to maintain non-violent resistance to Israeli occupation. The parties commit to pursuing an independent Palestinian state within the 1967 ceasefire lines.

2012 October - Local elections held on the West Bank undermine Fatah's political dominance. Fatah wins only two-fifths of the seats contested despite a 55% voter turnout. Lists led by Fatah rebels win control of four of the 11 major towns and cities. Independents and leftist candidates take control of a fifth municipality. Hamas boycotts the elections and prevents any voting in Gaza. Palestinians express hope that investing in technology start-ups will help lift them from economic stagnation. Features profile the West Bank's emerging tech start-up scene.

2012 November - The UN General Assembly upgrades Palestinian representation to "non-member observer state" status. The upgrade allows Palestinian representatives to participate in General Assembly debates. The new status improves Palestine's chances of joining additional UN agencies and international bodies.

2012 December - Fatah permits Hamas to hold a celebration rally on the West Bank marking the UN status upgrade. This represents a significant gesture of reconciliation from Fatah. Hamas reciprocates by allowing a Fatah rally in Gaza the following month.

2013 April - Prime Minister Salam Fayyad resigns following a long-standing personal and political dispute with Palestinian Authority Chairman Mahmoud Abbas. Academic administrator Rami Hamdallah succeeds Fayyad as prime minister in May.

2013 - Newly appointed US Secretary of State John Kerry launches an intensive series of shuttle diplomacy visits. Kerry aims to facilitate Israeli-Palestinian talks toward reaching a framework peace agreement by April 2014. Palestinian officials complain that Israel's continuing approval of Jewish housing construction in occupied East Jerusalem undermines negotiations. Israeli officials accuse the Palestinians of incitement and refusing to recognize Israel as a Jewish state.

2013 July - The fall of President Mohamed Morsi's government in Egypt dashes Palestinian hopes. Palestinians had expected Morsi's Muslim Brotherhood government to lift the Egyptian blockade of Gaza's border. Egyptian mediation in the Fatah-Hamas reconciliation process is suspended following the coup.

2013 December - Israel, Jordan, and the Palestinian Authority sign a trilateral water-sharing agreement. The pact aims to halt and eventually reverse the drying-out of the Dead Sea. Plans include laying a pipeline to carry brine from a Red Sea desalination plant. The project will simultaneously provide drinking water to the water-scarce region.

2014 March - Egypt's government formally bans all Hamas activities within Egyptian territory. Egyptian authorities seize Hamas assets because of the organization's links to Egypt's now-illegal Muslim Brotherhood.

2014 April - Fatah and Hamas reach yet another agreement to form a unity government. The unity government officially takes office in June with international recognition. Fatah leaders complain that a separate Hamas cabinet continues to rule Gaza independently.

2014 June - Three Jewish teenagers are kidnapped and murdered in the West Bank. Israel responds by conducting mass arrests of numerous Hamas members across the West Bank. Jewish extremists kidnap and kill a Palestinian teenager in apparent revenge. Militants in Gaza respond to the arrests and killing by firing increased rocket barrages toward Israel.

2014 July-August - Israel responds to escalating attacks from armed groups in Gaza with a major military campaign. The operation combines air strikes and a ground invasion to destroy missile launching sites. Israeli forces also target cross-border attack tunnels discovered under the border. The clashes result in over 2,000 Palestinian deaths, mostly civilians, and significant destruction in Gaza. Seventy-three Israelis, mostly soldiers, are killed. Fighting ends in an uneasy Egyptian-brokered ceasefire in August.
